openingProblem.problem: In 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union had just defeated Germany together. By 1949 they led rival armed blocs. What turned allies into rivals so quickly?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what broke the Grand Alliance?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: From Tehran to Potsdam: an alliance under strain, 1943–1945
chunks.body:
The Grand Alliance of the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union was a marriage of necessity against Nazi Germany. Even during the war it was strained. Stalin was furious at repeated delays to the "second front" in France and at one point recalled his ambassadors from London and Washington; the Soviets refused to help the Polish Home Army in the Warsaw Uprising of August 1944.

At **Tehran** (November–December 1943) the "Big Three" (Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin) agreed that the British and Americans would invade northern France by May 1944, and that the Soviet Union would eventually fight Japan. They also discussed the post-war map: Poland's eastern border would move west to the Curzon Line, and Poland would be compensated with German land up to the Oder and Neisse rivers. Roosevelt believed he had won Stalin's confidence; Stalin, meanwhile, gained concessions on Eastern Europe.

At **Yalta** (4–11 February 1945) the two sides traded. In return for entering the war against Japan, the Soviet Union was promised a sphere of influence in Manchuria, which the US Office of the Historian calls the conference's "major concrete accomplishment". The Western leaders accepted that the governments of Eastern Europe bordering the USSR should be "friendly" to Moscow, while Stalin pledged free elections in all liberated territories. These two promises could not both be kept. Roosevelt hoped that by meeting legitimate Soviet security needs he could turn the USSR into "an international team player".

Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945. By the end of April the new president, Harry Truman, had already clashed with the Soviets over Eastern Europe. At **Potsdam** (17 July–2 August 1945), with Attlee replacing Churchill midway, the victors confirmed four zones of occupation in a disarmed Germany, but quarrelled over reparations: Truman and his Secretary of State Byrnes insisted each power take reparations only from its own zone. On 24 July Truman told Stalin that the US had a powerful new bomb. Stalin, already informed by his spies, held firm. The Big Three never met again.

This mattered because the wartime agreements left the key question unresolved, which meant that "friendly" governments and "free elections" in Eastern Europe could be read in opposite ways once the common enemy was gone.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Wartime strains showed mistrust before the war ended.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The alliance still cooperated closely enough to defeat Germany.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yalta's promises on Eastern Europe were contradictory.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Soviets also made substantial concessions at Yalta.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Potsdam exposed disagreement over Germany and the bomb.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The powers still agreed on zones and demilitarisation.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent was ideology the main cause of the breakdown of the Grand Alliance between 1943 and 1949?

useItInAnEssay.claim: The wartime conferences contained the seeds of breakdown because their promises on Eastern Europe could not all be kept.
useItInAnEssay.prove: At Yalta the Western leaders accepted that East European governments should be 'friendly' to the USSR, while Stalin pledged free elections in all liberated territories.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that each side could later accuse the other of breaking the agreement, so the settlement became a source of conflict rather than a solution.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the alliance still achieved real cooperation: Soviet entry into the war against Japan and agreement on zones in Germany.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The conferences therefore postponed the conflict rather than causing it.

chunks.title: Fear, ideology and the atom, 1945–1947
chunks.body:
Once the war was won, each side read the other's actions through its own fears. The atomic bomb sharpened them. Some American officials hoped the US nuclear monopoly might make the Soviets more flexible in Europe or Asia, though Truman did not openly threaten Stalin. In 1965 the historian Gar Alperovitz went further, arguing that the bombing of Japan was intended to strengthen America's hand against the USSR; other scholars reject this. Either way, the Office of the Historian suggests, the atomic age probably made the Soviet Union "even more anxious to protect its borders with a controlled buffer zone".

Attempts to control the bomb failed. Under the **Baruch Plan** of June 1946 an international authority would control atomic energy, and the US would destroy its weapons only once the plan was fully in place. The Soviets rejected a scheme that let America keep its monopoly in the meantime and allowed inspection of Soviet sites; in December the USSR and Poland abstained and the plan died. The Soviet Union tested its own bomb in 1949.

Other disputes deepened mistrust in 1946. Soviet troops stayed in northern Iran, and Moscow pressed Iran for oil concessions and Turkey for rights in the Straits. In March 1946 Winston Churchill, speaking at Fulton, Missouri, gave his famous "iron curtain" speech, though, as Tony Judt notes, much of American opinion still wanted no alliance with anyone.

American policy hardened in 1947. The diplomat George Kennan's "X-Article" called for "a long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment of Russian expansive tendencies". When Britain announced that it could no longer support the Greek government against Communist rebels, Truman asked Congress on 12 March 1947 for $400 million for Greece and Turkey and declared that the US would "support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures". This was the **Truman Doctrine**, an ideological framing of the conflict as freedom against totalitarianism. Yet Stalin had in fact refused to support the Greek Communists, and Judt argues that the Doctrine "had remarkably little impact on Soviet calculations".

This mattered because ideology and fear reinforced each other: each side's defensive moves looked like aggression to the other, which meant that by 1947 cooperation had given way to containment.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The atomic monopoly increased Soviet insecurity.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Truman did not use the bomb to threaten Stalin openly.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Soviet actions in Iran and Turkey convinced Washington of Soviet expansionism.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: These were pressures on neighbours, not a plan for world revolution.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Truman Doctrine framed the conflict in ideological terms.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt says it hardly changed Soviet calculations.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Fear, more than ideology, drove the breakdown in 1946–47, because each side saw the other's security measures as aggression.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The Soviets rejected the Baruch Plan of 1946 because it let the US keep its nuclear monopoly, while Washington saw Soviet pressure on Iran and Turkey as expansion.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that defensive moves on one side confirmed the worst fears of the other, so each step led to a harder response.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, ideology shaped how those fears were expressed: the Truman Doctrine of 1947 described a struggle of free peoples against totalitarianism.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Fear was therefore the engine of the breakdown, and ideology its language.

chunks.title: Money and camps: the Marshall Plan and the Soviet response, 1947–1948
chunks.body:
Economic interests turned rivalry into division. On 5 June 1947 Secretary of State George Marshall called for a programme to rebuild Europe. Congress approved it in March 1948, and aid eventually rose to over $12 billion. The plan helped Europe's recovery, but it also served American interests: it created markets for American goods and, as the Office of the Historian puts it, drew participating states into the United States' economic orbit as "a bulwark against Communism".

Eastern Europe was invited too. Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria and Albania all showed initial interest. But at the Paris talks the Soviet foreign minister, Molotov, walked out on 2 July 1947, and no future Communist state received a dollar of Marshall aid. The Soviets feared American economic domination of their satellites, and Stalin was unwilling to open his closed society to Western inspection.

Stalin's answer was ideological discipline. In September 1947 he set up the **Cominform** at Szklarska Poręba in Poland. Its real purpose, Judt argues, was to re-establish Soviet control of the Communist movement. Zhdanov, the Soviet delegate, described the world as divided into two camps, and Communist parties everywhere switched to confrontation: strikes, campaigns against the Marshall Plan and, in Eastern Europe, a faster seizure of power. Since 1946 Communists there had found they could not win through the ballot box, so they used intimidation and terror against their opponents.

The decisive moment came in **February 1948**, when the Communists seized power in Czechoslovakia, a more or less democratic country that had seemed friendly to Moscow. Judt calls the Prague coup the signal of Stalin's acceptance of "the inevitability of confrontation rather than agreement with the West". It galvanised the West: in March Britain, France and the Benelux countries formed the Brussels Pact, and the London Conference agreed to extend the Marshall Plan to western Germany and plan a West German state. On 20 March the Soviet representative walked out of the Allied Control Council. "The real Cold War in Europe," Judt writes, "had begun."

This mattered because economic aid and the Soviet refusal of it drew a line through Europe, which meant that recovery in the West and Sovietisation in the East became two sides of the same division.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Marshall Plan served American economic and political interests.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It was also a great humanitarian effort, and the East was invited.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Soviet refusal of Marshall aid divided Europe.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Stalin had good reason to fear US economic domination.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Cominform and the Prague coup imposed Soviet control in the East.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Communists in Eastern Europe were already using terror before 1947.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the significance of economic interests in the emergence of superpower rivalry in Europe between 1947 and 1949.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Economic interests were central to the division of Europe because the Marshall Plan forced every state to choose a side.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Marshall offered aid to all of Europe in June 1947, but Molotov walked out on 2 July and no future Communist state received a dollar.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that economic recovery became a test of loyalty, so the West was drawn into America's economic orbit while the East was tied to Moscow.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Soviet response was political as much as economic: the Cominform of September 1947 and the Prague coup of February 1948 imposed control by force.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Economics therefore drew the line through Europe, but politics and force made it permanent.

chunks.title: Blockade, NATO and China: rivalry in Europe and Asia, 1948–1949
chunks.body:
The breakdown reached its climax over Germany. In June 1948 the US and Britain introduced a new currency, the Deutschmark, in their zones and in West Berlin without telling the Soviets. From 24 June Soviet forces blockaded West Berlin by land and water. The Western powers answered with an airlift that, at its height, landed a plane every 45 seconds at Tempelhof airport, and Truman sent to Britain B-29 bombers capable of carrying nuclear weapons. In May 1949 Moscow lifted the blockade. The crisis, in the Office of the Historian's words, "solidified the division of Europe": the Western powers created **NATO** in 1949, the first peacetime alliance the US had joined outside the Western Hemisphere, and two separate German states followed.

Rivalry spread to Asia. At Yalta the USSR had won a sphere of influence in Manchuria; after Japan's surrender it occupied Manchuria and left only when Chinese Communist forces were in place, while the US flew Nationalist troops into Japanese-held territory. General Marshall tried and failed to broker a coalition government, and by 1946 China was in all-out civil war. On 1 October 1949 **Mao Zedong** proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan. The US suspended relations with the new state, and Truman faced charges of having "lost" China.

How do the two superpowers' roles compare? Both acted from security fears and both used economic and military tools to build a bloc. The US used aid (the Marshall Plan) and alliances (NATO); the USSR used control of local Communist parties, the Cominform and, in Czechoslovakia, a coup. But Judt places the main responsibility on Moscow: the division of Germany and Europe lay "in Stalin's own errors", and the Cold War in Europe was "an unavoidable outcome of the Soviet dictator's personality and the system over which he ruled". Had Stalin accepted the Marshall Plan in 1947, Judt suggests, he could have shifted the balance of Europe. Judt also warns that the Americans, like Stalin, "were improvising", and that there is "little to be gained from asking 'who started the Cold War?'"

This mattered because by the end of 1949 two armed blocs faced each other in Europe and a Communist China had appeared in Asia, which meant that the Grand Alliance had given way to a global superpower rivalry.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Berlin crisis and NATO turned division into armed confrontation.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The airlift avoided war: neither side fired a shot.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Chinese Revolution extended rivalry to Asia.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Communists won mainly through their own strength in a civil war.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Judt places the main responsibility on Stalin's errors and system.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt also says both sides were improvising.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Both superpowers built blocs between 1947 and 1949, but they did so by different means.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The US used the Marshall Plan and, in 1949, NATO, while the USSR used the Cominform, the Prague coup of February 1948 and the Berlin blockade.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the West was bound by aid and alliance, whereas the East was held together by party control and force.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, both sides acted from security fears, and Judt argues that the Americans, like Stalin, were improvising.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The difference in methods therefore matters more than the similarity in motives, which is why Judt places the main responsibility on Stalin.

historiography.argument: The division of Europe lay 'in Stalin's own errors': the Cold War in Europe was 'an unavoidable outcome of the Soviet dictator's personality and the system over which he ruled', and the Truman Doctrine 'had remarkably little impact on Soviet calculations'.
historiography.useItLikeThis: Judt's view supports the claim that the USSR bore the main responsibility, which suggests the Marshall Plan refusal, not American rhetoric, was the turning point.

historiography.argument: In 1965 Alperovitz argued that the atomic bombing of Japan was intended to gain a stronger position for post-war bargaining with the Soviet Union (as summarised by the Office of the Historian; other scholars disagree).
historiography.useItLikeThis: Alperovitz's view supports the claim that American atomic diplomacy deepened Soviet fears, which suggests the US shared responsibility for the breakdown.

misconceptions.wrong: The Cold War began only after the war ended.
misconceptions.right: The alliance was **strained during the war**: the second front and the Warsaw Uprising.

misconceptions.wrong: Eastern Europe was never offered Marshall aid.
misconceptions.right: It was invited, and Poland and Czechoslovakia showed interest, but none took part after **Molotov walked out** on 2 July 1947.

misconceptions.wrong: The Truman Doctrine changed Stalin's policy.
misconceptions.right: Judt: it had **remarkably little impact** on Soviet calculations.

misconceptions.wrong: Superpower rivalry before 1950 was only about Europe.
misconceptions.right: It spread to **Asia**: Manchuria, the Chinese civil war and the PRC in 1949.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was ideology the main cause of the breakdown of the Grand Alliance between 1943 and 1949?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.scope: The breakdown of the Grand Alliance
decodeKey.judgement: Whether ideology outweighed fear and economic interests

modelPlan.thesis: Ideology shaped how each side saw the other, but mutual fear, sharpened by the bomb and by Soviet pressure on its neighbours, and the economic division created by the Marshall Plan did more to break the alliance.

arguments.claim: Ideology: the Truman Doctrine and the two camps (named factor first).
Fear: the bomb and the Baruch Plan.
Fear: Soviet pressure on Iran and Turkey.
Economic interests: the Marshall Plan.

modelPlan.counter: The alliance had been strained during the war over the second front, before ideology came to the fore.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: What turned disagreement into division? The economic test of the Marshall Plan in 1947, which ideology then justified.

segments.text: Ideology gave the breakdown its language, but it was not the main cause.
The Truman Doctrine of March 1947 spoke of 'free peoples' and Zhdanov of two camps, yet Stalin had refused to support the Greek Communists.
This meant that ideological rhetoric described a conflict already driven by other forces, so it hardened the division rather than starting it.
However, fear of the bomb and of Soviet expansion, and the Marshall Plan's economic test, did more to force the break in 1947–48.
Ideology was therefore a secondary cause that turned a power struggle into a contest of systems.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The Soviet Union was more responsible than the United States for the breakdown of the Grand Alliance.” Discuss with reference to the period 1945 to 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: the USSR was more responsible
decodeKey.scope: The breakdown of the Grand Alliance
decodeKey.judgement: Whose actions turned rivalry into division

modelPlan.thesis: The USSR bore more responsibility, because Stalin's refusal of Marshall aid, the Cominform and the Prague coup turned rivalry into division; but American atomic diplomacy and ideological rhetoric deepened Soviet fears.

arguments.claim: For: refusal of Marshall aid and the Cominform.
For: terror in Eastern Europe and the Prague coup.
Against: atomic diplomacy and the Baruch Plan.
Against: the Deutschmark and the London plans.

modelPlan.counter: Judt warns that both sides were improvising, so 'who started it' may be the wrong question.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Whose decisions made division unavoidable? Stalin's, Judt argues, because accepting Marshall aid could have changed the balance in 1947.

segments.text: The Soviet Union was more responsible, because Stalin's decisions turned rivalry into division.
Molotov walked out of the Marshall Plan talks in July 1947, the Cominform followed in September, and in February 1948 the Communists seized power in Prague.
This meant that Stalin closed off the possibility of a shared European recovery, so the West concluded it faced a bloc held together by force.
However, the US monopoly of the bomb and the Baruch Plan increased Soviet insecurity, as Alperovitz argues, and the West introduced the Deutschmark without consulting Moscow.
The claim is therefore largely valid, as Judt concludes, though both sides acted from fear.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the roles of the United States and the Soviet Union in the emergence of superpower rivalry between 1945 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The roles of the two superpowers

modelPlan.thesis: Both superpowers acted from security fears and built blocs, but the US did so through aid and alliance while the USSR relied on party control and force, which is why the Soviet role did more to make division permanent.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both acted from security fears.
Similarity: both built blocs with economic tools.
Difference: aid and alliance against party control.
Difference: persuasion against force.

modelPlan.counter: The US also used pressure: the Deutschmark was introduced without consulting the Soviets.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Methods: force in Prague and Berlin made division harder to undo than Marshall aid.

segments.text: Both superpowers built blocs from fear, but by very different methods.
The US offered Marshall aid and in 1949 joined NATO, whereas the USSR founded the Cominform and backed the Prague coup of February 1948.
This meant that the Western bloc rested on aid and alliance, while the Eastern bloc rested on party control and force.
However, the US also acted unilaterally, introducing the Deutschmark in June 1948 without telling the Soviets.
The decisive difference was therefore in methods, which is why Judt places the main responsibility on Stalin.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the significance of economic interests in the emergence of superpower rivalry in Europe between 1947 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far economics, rather than security or ideology, explains the division

modelPlan.thesis: Economic interests were highly significant, because the Marshall Plan turned recovery into a test of loyalty that divided Europe; but the Soviet response was political, and force made the division permanent.

arguments.claim: The Marshall Plan and American markets.
Soviet refusal and the economic division.
Western Germany's recovery and the currency.
Limits: the Cominform and the Prague coup were political.

modelPlan.counter: Security fears, shown in the Brussels Pact and NATO, explain the military division of Europe.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did economics cause the division or only reveal it? It caused the decisive break in 1947, when states had to choose.

segments.text: Economic interests were central to the emergence of rivalry in Europe.
The Marshall Plan created markets for American goods, and after Molotov's walk-out in July 1947 no Communist state received a dollar.
This meant that recovery became a test of loyalty, so the West was drawn into America's economic orbit and the East tied to Moscow.
However, the Soviet answer was political: the Cominform and the Prague coup imposed control by force.
Economic interests were therefore the trigger of division, while political force made it permanent.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the division of Germany between 1945 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: Germany was divided mainly because the Western powers chose to rebuild their zones with Marshall aid and a new currency, which Stalin answered with the blockade; the main consequence was the military division of Europe through NATO.

arguments.claim: Cause: reparations and zones at Potsdam.
Cause: the London plans and the Deutschmark.
Consequence: the blockade and airlift.
Consequence: NATO and two German states.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues that a divided Germany was probably preferred by all parties to a united Germany hostile to them.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The military division of Europe, symbolised by NATO.

segments.text: Germany was divided mainly because the Western powers decided to rebuild their zones without the USSR.
The London Conference of 1948 extended the Marshall Plan to western Germany, and in June the Deutschmark was introduced without informing the Soviets.
This meant that the occupation zones became separate economies, so Stalin's blockade from 24 June 1948 was a response to a division already under way.
However, Judt argues that Stalin's own rigidity squandered his chance of a united, neutral Germany.
Division therefore had causes on both sides, and its main consequence was NATO and two German states in 1949.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why superpower rivalry spread to Asia between 1945 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.factorOrTask: Reasons for the spread of rivalry
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Rivalry spread to Asia because the wartime bargain gave the USSR a foothold in Manchuria, both powers backed rival sides in China's civil war, and the Communist victory of 1949 made China a Cold War issue in American politics.

arguments.claim: The Yalta bargain over Manchuria.
Rival support in the Chinese civil war.
The Communist victory and the 'loss' of China.
US hegemony in occupied Japan.

modelPlan.counter: The Chinese civil war had its own roots in decades of conflict between Nationalists and Communists.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? The Communist victory of 1949, because it turned China into a superpower issue.

segments.text: Rivalry spread to Asia mainly because the two superpowers backed opposite sides in China's civil war.
After Japan's surrender the US flew Nationalist troops into Japanese-held territory, while the USSR left Manchuria only when Chinese Communist forces were in place.
This meant that a civil war became a contest between the blocs, so the Communist victory of October 1949 was seen in Washington as a Cold War defeat.
However, the civil war had its own roots, and General Marshall had tried to broker a coalition government.
The superpowers therefore did not create the conflict in China, but they turned it into part of their rivalry.
